docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the Humidity Sensing Subsystem I designed for Team 202's Environmental Monitoring Device in EGR 304. It walks through the design from block diagram to component selection, schematic, and power budget, so a reader can understand what the board does, why each part was chosen, and how it connects to the rest of the team's system.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Team 202 is building an Environmental Monitoring Device: a set of four connected boards that each measure part of the surrounding environment and report it to a central hub board with an LCD display. Each teammate designs their own board, and the boards share data over an 8-wire ribbon cable using the class connector standard.

My board measures relative humidity. A Sensirion SHT31-ARP-B analog sensor produces a voltage proportional to humidity, an MCP6001 op amp amplifies it, an RC low-pass filter removes noise, and the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano converts it to a number. The PIC then sends the humidity reading to Zander Boward's hub board over UART, where it is displayed.

See the full system in our team report.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page shows the block diagram for my subsystem on Team 202's Environmental Monitoring Device. My board measures relative humidity and sends the reading to Zander Boward's hub board, which shows it on the LCD.

  • Power levels: A 9 V DC wall adapter powers the board through a barrel jack. An STMicroelectronics L7805CV linear regulator steps this down to a regulated 5 V (1.5 A max), which powers the Curiosity Nano, the humidity sensor, and the op amp.
  • Sensor: A Sensirion SHT31-ARP-B humidity sensor outputs an analog voltage from 0.5 V (0 %RH) to 4.5 V (100 %RH). The signal passes through an op amp buffer (Microchip MCP6001T-I/OT) and a passive RC low-pass filter (fc ≈ 16 Hz) before reaching the ADC on pin RA0 of the PIC18F57Q43.
  • Actuator: None. This subsystem is sensing only.
  • Team connections: Connector 1 (2x4 IDC, 8-wire ribbon cable) connects to Zander's hub board. Pin 1 sends humidity data to the hub (UART TX, RC2), pin 2 receives data from the hub (UART RX, RC3), pin 8 is ground, and pins 3-7 are not connected.
  • Power source: 9 V DC wall adapter through a CUI Devices PJ-002A barrel jack.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Team 202: Environmental Monitoring Device Sidra Elsaady: Humidity Sensing Subsystem (Sensor)

This page compares at least three candidate solutions for each major block in my subsystem's block diagram, then gives the part I selected and why. Every selection below belongs to the Humidity Sensing Subsystem unless noted otherwise.

The Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano was selected for us, so it does not get a selection table (it is still included in the power budget). Passives, connectors, pushbuttons, standard LEDs and fuses are excluded from the assignment.

docs.title: 1. Humidity Sensor — Humidity Sensing Subsystem
docs.text:
1. Sensirion SHT31-ARP-B analog humidity/temperature sensor

    • $5.00/each (Digi-Key)
    • SHT31-ARP-B on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons ±2 %RH typical accuracy, which beats our ±3 %RH requirement (PR 2.1) 2.5 × 2.5 mm DFN-8 package with no leads, so hand soldering needs extended pads, flux and a fine-tip iron (hot air is easier if available) Factory calibrated, so no humidity chamber is needed to calibrate it Output can source/sink only ±100 µA, so it needs a high-impedance buffer before the filter and ADC Ratiometric analog output (10–90 % of VDD) shares the same 5 V reference as the PIC ADC, so supply drift cancels out Sensitive to heat from nearby parts, so it must be placed away from the L7805 regulator Runs on 2.4–5.5 V, so it works directly from our 5 V rail Low supply current (350 µA max) Analog output gives our subsystem a real signal-conditioning path (buffer + filter + ADC), as the project brief requires In stock at multiple authorized distributors

  2. Honeywell HIH-4000-001 analog humidity sensor

    • $241.59/each (Digi-Key)
    • HIH-4000-001 on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons 3-pin through-hole SIP package that is easy to hand solder ±3.5 %RH accuracy does not meet our ±3 %RH requirement Designed for a 5 V supply (4–5.8 V), matching our rail Very expensive for one sensor ($241.59 at Digi-Key), with one Digi-Key listing marked not available and a 99-week lead time at another distributor Near-linear analog voltage output that goes straight to the ADC Needs temperature compensation in firmware for best accuracy, and we have no separate temperature reading Long industry track record with lots of example circuits Larger, so it takes more space near the enclosure vent

  3. Custom: TE Connectivity HPP801A031 (HS1101LF) capacitive humidity sensor + 555 timer oscillator

    • about $9 in total
    • HPP801A031 (HS1101LF) on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons Through-hole leads that are easy to solder Not factory calibrated; capacitance-to-RH conversion needs a curve fit and calibration with a reference hygrometer Frequency output can be measured with a PIC timer, which is immune to analog noise on the ribbon cable Rated ±2 %RH for the sensor alone, but the full circuit's accuracy depends on our own oscillator and calibration, which makes PR 2.1 hard to verify Building the oscillator ourselves demonstrates custom circuit design More parts (timer IC + precision resistors) and more board area Limited stock at major distributors at time of research

Choice: Option 1: Sensirion SHT31-ARP-B

Rationale: The SHT31-ARP-B is the only option that meets the ±3 %RH accuracy requirement out of the box, because it is factory calibrated at ±2 %RH. Its ratiometric output scales with the same 5 V rail that the PIC ADC uses as a reference, so small regulator variations don't show up as humidity errors. The analog output also fits the course requirement to condition a real-world signal before digitizing it. The HIH-4000 is easier to solder, but it misses the accuracy spec and costs about 48 times as much on Digi-Key with very limited availability. The HS1101LF would need a calibration process we can't verify against PR 2.1. The main risk with the SHT31 is its DFN package. We will reduce that risk by extending the footprint's pads about 0.75 mm past the package so they can be soldered with a fine-tip iron and flux, and by adding a via under the center pad so it can be soldered from the back of the board. The center pad is only needed for mechanical strength (it is internally tied to VSS, per datasheet §3.4). If the lab's hot-air station or reflow oven is available we will use it instead, and we will order spares at $5 each.

docs.title: 2. Signal Amplifier (Op Amp) — Humidity Sensing Subsystem
docs.text:
1. Microchip MCP6001T-I/OT single rail-to-rail op amp (SOT-23-5)

    • =$0.30/each
    • MCP6001T-I/OT on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons Rail-to-rail input and output, so it passes the full 0.5–4.5 V sensor range on a single 5 V supply SOT-23-5 is small (0.95 mm pitch) but still hand-solderable Very low quiescent current (100 µA typical, 170 µA max) Only one amplifier per package, so a second filter stage would need another chip Runs on 1.8–6.0 V, so it works on our 5 V rail 1 MHz GBW is more than enough here but limits reuse for faster signals Very high input impedance doesn't load the SHT31's ±100 µA output Same manufacturer as the PIC, with lots of application notes and a SPICE model

  2. Microchip MCP6002-I/P dual rail-to-rail op amp (PDIP-8)

    • = $0.45/each
    • MCP6002-I/P on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons Same rail-to-rail performance and 100 µA per amplifier as the MCP6001 Much larger footprint than SOT-23-5 Through-hole DIP package is the easiest to solder and can be socketed for replacement Unused second amplifier must be tied off properly to avoid oscillation The second amplifier could build an active low-pass filter Roughly doubles quiescent current if both amplifiers are powered

  3. Texas Instruments LM358P dual general-purpose op amp (PDIP-8)

    • = $0.35/each
    • LM358P on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons Very common and inexpensive, with many second sources Output is not rail-to-rail; on a 5 V supply it only reaches about 3.5 V, so readings above roughly 75 %RH would clip Through-hole package that is easy to solder Input common-mode range does not reach the positive rail Wide supply range (3–32 V) Higher supply current (about 0.7 mA typical) than the MCP600x parts

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6001T-I/OT

Rationale: The buffer must pass the sensor's full 0.5–4.5 V output on a single 5 V supply without loading the sensor. The MCP6001's rail-to-rail input and output does this, and its 170 µA max draw barely affects the power budget. The LM358 was rejected because its output saturates around 3.5 V, which would cut off the top quarter of the humidity range. The MCP6002 is electrically equivalent and easier to solder. It stays as a drop-in backup if a second-order active filter is needed later, but for a single unity-gain buffer the smaller single-amplifier MCP6001 saves board area near the sensor.

docs.title: 3. Low-Pass Filter — Humidity Sensing Subsystem
docs.text:
The filter block is built from passives, which the assignment excludes. It is included here briefly because it is a block on my diagram.

  1. Passive first-order RC filter (fc = 16 Hz)

    • = $0.10 in parts
    Pros Cons Only two parts, no extra power draw Only −20 dB/decade roll-off Humidity changes slowly (8 s response time), so a 16 Hz cutoff removes noise without hiding real changes Output impedance of the RC slightly affects ADC acquisition time The capacitor also serves as the ADC's charge reservoir during sampling

  2. Active second-order Sallen-Key filter using the second half of an MCP6002

    • = $0.45 + passives
    Pros Cons −40 dB/decade roll-off with low output impedance More parts and tuning for little benefit on a slow signal Reuses the spare amplifier if the MCP6002 is chosen Requires changing to a dual op amp

  3. Firmware-only filtering (moving average in the PIC, or the ADCC's built-in averaging mode)

    Pros Cons No hardware cost; the ADCC can average automatically Does not prevent aliasing of high-frequency noise picked up before the ADC Filter strength can be changed in code without a board revision Doesn't satisfy the project's analog signal-conditioning requirement on its own

Choice: Option 1 in hardware, plus Option 3 ADCC averaging in firmware.

Rationale: The RC filter is the simplest solution that removes noise well above the sensor's bandwidth, while the ADCC averaging smooths the remaining noise at no cost and still updates far faster than the 2 s requirement.

docs.title: 4. 5 V Voltage Regulator — Humidity Sensing Subsystem power
docs.text:
1. STMicroelectronics L7805CV 5 V linear regulator (TO-220)

    • $1.08/each (Digi-Key)
    • L7805CV on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons 1.5 A output is far above our 31.9 mA budget (with 25% margin) Needs about 2 V of headroom (dropout), so input must stay above 7 V Built-in short-circuit current limiting and thermal shutdown support PR 6.1 and PR 6.2 Wastes (9 − 5) V × I as heat (about 0.13 W at our budget, so no heatsink is needed) Through-hole TO-220 is easy to solder and can take a heatsink Quiescent current up to 8 mA Same regulator as the rest of Team 202, so spare parts and layouts are shared

  2. Texas Instruments LM2940CT-5.0 low-dropout regulator (TO-220)

    • $0.71/each at 1,000 units from TI (LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB); about 2.04 USD for one from Mouser
    • LM2940CT-5.0 on Texas Instruments
    Pros Cons Only about 0.5 V dropout, so it keeps working as a supply sags Costs nearly twice as much as the L7805 when buying just one (about 2.04 USD vs 1.08 USD) Reverse-battery and overvoltage protection built in Needs a large output capacitor (≥ 22 µF) with controlled ESR for stability 1 A output, also through-hole Low dropout gives no benefit with a 9 V input

  3. STMicroelectronics LD1117V50 5 V LDO (TO-220)

    • $0.57/each (Digi-Key)
    • LD1117V50 on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons About 1 V dropout, at low cost Only 800 mA output Same family as the LD1117V33 used on the team hub board Different pinout from the 78xx (GND/OUT/IN), which is a common layout mistake Needs a 10 µF output capacitor for stability

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV

Rationale: With a fixed 9 V input there is 4 V of headroom, so the L7805's 2 V dropout is not a limitation and the extra cost of an LDO buys nothing. Its built-in current limit and thermal shutdown directly support our safety requirements, and at our 31.9 mA budget it dissipates only about 0.13 W, so it needs no heatsink. Using the same regulator as the rest of the team also simplifies layout reviews and spare parts.

docs.title: 5. Power Source — Humidity Sensing Subsystem power
docs.text:
1. CUI Devices SWI12-9-N-P5 9 V 1.2 A wall adapter (5.5 × 2.1 mm plug)

    • =$17.59/each
    • SWI12-9-N-P5 on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons Regulated 9 V output with plenty of current margin (1.2 A vs 39.9 mA needed) Requires an outlet near the device Standard 5.5 × 2.1 mm center-positive plug More expensive than smaller adapters Safety-certified supply from a reputable manufacturer The course's PJ-002A jack has a 2.0 mm center pin, so the 2.1 mm plug fit must be checked before ordering No batteries to drain during long demos

  2. Bel Power Solutions SWI6-9-N-P5 9 V 0.67 A wall adapter

    • $16.13/each (Digi-Key)
    • SWI6-9-N-P5 on Digi-Key
    Pros Cons Still about 16 times the 39.9 mA my board needs Less margin if the team ever powers more than one board from one adapter Smaller and slightly less expensive than the 12 W version Requires an outlet Same plug and polarity

  3. Adafruit 248 6 × AA battery holder with 5.5 × 2.1 mm plug (=9 V)

    • $2.50/each + batteries
    • Adafruit 6 × AA holder
    Pros Cons Portable, matching the replaceable-battery goal in PR 1.3 Voltage falls from about 9.6 V to 6 V as cells discharge, dropping below the L7805's ~7 V minimum input well before the cells are empty No mains wiring Batteries are an ongoing cost

Choice: Option 1: CUI Devices SWI12-9-N-P5 9 V 1.2 A wall adapter

Rationale: The course requires a 9 V supply through a barrel jack, and a regulated wall adapter keeps the L7805 input steady for accurate ratiometric readings. The 1.2 A rating leaves a large margin over my 39.9 mA draw and stays below the team's 1.5 A input limit (PR 6.1). A battery pack would drop below the L7805's dropout limit partway through discharge, which would cause the 5 V rail and the humidity reading to drift.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A power budget adds up the worst-case current every part of my board can draw, so I can check that the regulator, the fuse, and the wall adapter are sized correctly and that nothing will overheat. I listed every part that draws current on the regulated +5 V rail: the Curiosity Nano, the SHT31-ARP-B humidity sensor, the MCP6001 op amp and its gain resistors, the three indicator LEDs, the UART level-shift divider, and the button and reset pull-ups. Each value is the maximum current from the part's datasheet, or a worst-case calculation for resistors and LEDs. I then added a 25 % safety margin and carried the result back to the +9 V input rail, where the L7805CV's own quiescent current is added.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
From the prepared power budget:

  • +5 V rail: the board draws at most 39.8 mA, or 49.7 mA with a 25 % margin. The L7805CV can supply 1.5 A, leaving about 1.45 A unused, so the regulator is far from its limit. The three LEDs are the largest load (about 29 mA together), more than the microcontroller itself.
  • +9 V input: including the L7805's 8 mA quiescent current, the board needs at most 59.7 mA from the wall adapter. The CUI SWI12-9-N-P5 is rated for 1.2 A, so it has plenty of headroom, and the board stays well under the team's 1.5 A input limit (PR 6.1).
  • Fuse: the 500 mA fuse is about 8× the worst-case input current. It will not blow during normal operation, and it will still open on a short circuit.
  • Regulator heat: the L7805 dissipates about 0.27 W. With the TO-220's 50 °C/W junction-to-ambient rating, that is only about a 14 °C rise, so no heatsink is needed. Its minimum load of 5 mA is always met.
  • Total board power is about 0.54 W from the 9 V supply.
  • UART level: Team 202 uses 3.3 V UART, so the R4/R5 divider that shifts the PIC's 5 V TX down to about 3.2 V is included (about 1 mA while TX is high).
